slides.label: Differentiation
slides.notes: Open by making the word differentiation concrete for forms. Earlier chapters gave measurement devices: functions read points, one-forms read directed motion, two-forms read oriented area, and three-forms read oriented volume. Chapter 36 asks what it means for those meters to vary from point to point. The exterior derivative is the operation that turns that local variation into the next kind of measurement.

slides.label: Exterior Derivative As Boundary Detector
slides.notes: Present d as a boundary detector rather than as a symbolic decoration. A p-form is evaluated on small p-dimensional probes. Its exterior derivative is evaluated on one-dimension-larger probes and records the first-order failure of the original form's boundary readings to cancel. This is the small-scale reason Stokes' theorem will later identify a bulk integral of d omega with a boundary integral of omega.

slides.label: d Of A One-Form: Circulation Cell
slides.notes: Use the circulation cell to anchor the first formula. A one-form alpha equals P dx plus Q dy. Walk around a tiny coordinate rectangle and add the edge readings. The horizontal edges compare Q in the x direction and the vertical edges compare P in the y direction, with orientation deciding the signs. Dividing by area leaves Q_x minus P_y, the coefficient of dx wedge dy.

slides.label: Coordinates: Variation Becomes The Next Form
slides.notes: This slide generalizes the local cell calculation. The exterior derivative differentiates each coefficient, wedges in the coordinate direction of variation, and then collects terms using alternation. For a one-form this produces the curl-like area reader. For a two-form in three dimensions it produces the divergence-like volume reader. The key teaching point is that d does not merely take derivatives; it upgrades the probe dimension.

slides.label: The Graded Product Rule
slides.notes: The product rule for forms must remember degree. When d passes across a p-form alpha to differentiate beta, it crosses p one-form slots, so the second term receives the sign minus one to the p. Students should see the sign as orientation bookkeeping, not as a convention to memorize. The local figure names the object, visual, formula, and check stages for that bookkeeping.

slides.label: Why d Squared Is Zero
slides.notes: Make d squared equals zero feel geometric before it feels algebraic. Algebraically, second partial derivatives appear in opposite wedge orders and cancel when the coefficients are smooth. Geometrically, the boundary of a boundary has no remaining edge: each codimension-two piece is visited twice with opposite orientation. This cancellation is the hinge between exact, closed, and later cohomological language.

slides.label: Closed Versus Exact
slides.notes: Define the two adjectives through d. A form is closed when d omega equals zero, so the local boundary detector finds no first-order variation. A form is exact when omega is already d eta for some lower-degree form. Exact always implies closed because d squared is zero, but the reverse can fail globally when topology leaves noncontractible loops or holes for integrals to detect.

slides.label: Cauchy-Riemann As Closedness
slides.notes: This is a compact application: complex differentiability can be translated into closed real one-forms. If f equals u plus i v, the real and imaginary parts of f dz are u dx minus v dy and v dx plus u dy. Requiring both to be closed gives u_x equals v_y and u_y equals minus v_x. Exterior differentiation packages the compatibility equations as a cancellation test.

slides.label: Vector Calculus And Maxwell Fit The Ladder
slides.notes: Use the ladder to connect familiar vector calculus to the forms sequence. With a metric and orientation in the background, d on zero-forms becomes gradient, d on one-forms becomes curl, and d on two-forms becomes divergence. Maxwell's compact equations use the same language: dF equals zero for the homogeneous equations, while d star F equals J after the Hodge star inserts the metric.

slides.label: Stokes-Style Takeaways
slides.notes: Close by returning to the lesson's governing image: exterior differentiation detects what boundary readings fail to cancel. On a small cell, that is a derivative coefficient. On a region, Stokes' theorem turns the accumulated d omega reading into a boundary omega reading. The class should leave knowing the formulas, but more importantly knowing why the operation raises degree and why d squared must vanish.
